https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/vulcan-st.plain_summary: Vulcan Energy is building a 30-megawatt (MW) geothermal power plant in Landau, Germany that will extract heat from hot rocks deep underground to generate electricity and heat. The facility, part of a larger project called Lionheart, will also extract lithium (a valuable mineral used in batteries) from hot mineral-rich water that comes up from the same deep wells, making it a combined energy and mineral extraction operation. Early construction work on foundations and roads has started, with full construction expected to begin by 2027.

second drilling site operational by mid-2026

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/5-mw-geot.title: 5-MW geothermal pilot project in Meshginshahr, Iran starts grid supply
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/5-mw-geot.plain_summary: Iran has successfully started operating its first geothermal power plant in Meshginshahr, which generates 5.4 megawatts of electricity by harnessing heat from deep underground rock. The plant taps into a geothermal reservoir (hot rock formations beneath the surface) estimated to hold enough energy for 250 megawatts total, with wells drilled to depths of 3,000 meters already capable of supporting 30 megawatts of production. After decades of planning and exploration starting in 1975, this pilot project represents a major milestone for Iran's renewable energy development.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.title: Drilling of geothermal research well starts in Cologne-Dellbrück, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.plain_summary: Germany has begun drilling an exploratory well in Cologne to test whether limestone layers deep underground can be used as geothermal reservoirs (natural underground storage areas for hot water). Researchers will drill down to 1,000 meters and collect rock samples to check if the limestone contains natural cavities and cracks that could hold warm water suitable for heating. The data gathered will help municipalities across the region understand whether they can tap into geothermal energy resources beneath their communities.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field demonstration and integrated productivity-economics assessment of multi-lateral geothermal wells enabled by directional steel shot drilling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers conducted a real-world test of geothermal wells that branch out in multiple directions underground (called multi-lateral wells) using a specialized drilling technique with steel shot pellets instead of traditional drill bits. The study examined whether this directional drilling approach works effectively and whether it makes economic sense financially for geothermal energy production.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Influence of fluid-rock interactions on mechanical, thermal and transport properties of sandstone reservoir during geothermal waste fluid reinjection
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how hot geothermal fluids (water heated by Earth's interior) interact with sandstone rock when pumped back underground after energy extraction, focusing on how these interactions change the rock's strength, heat capacity, and ability to allow fluid flow. Understanding these changes is important for superhot rock geothermal systems that rely on reinjecting cooled fluids to maintain long-term productivity and prevent damage to the reservoir.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Experimental study of anisotropic behavior of biotite-ordered granite under thermally-coupled true triaxial compression conditions in deep geothermal boreholes
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how granite rock behaves when exposed to extreme heat and pressure deep underground, similar to conditions found in geothermal boreholes (holes drilled into the earth to access hot rock). They focused on biotite-ordered granite (a type of crystalline rock containing the mineral biotite) and tested how it responds differently depending on the direction of applied forces, which is important for understanding rock stability during superhot rock geothermal drilling and extraction.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermo-hydraulic drivers of superhot geothermal well performance
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research article examines how heat and fluid flow work together to affect how superhot geothermal wells (wells drilled into extremely hot underground rock) perform. The study, published in a peer-reviewed geothermal journal, explores the technical factors that determine whether these high-temperature wells can effectively extract energy from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Damage evolution of thermal shock in granite for enhanced geothermal systems
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how granite rock breaks down when exposed to repeated heating and cooling cycles, which is important for enhanced geothermal systems (engineered reservoirs created by fracturing hot rock underground to extract heat). Understanding this damage process helps engineers design better methods to create and maintain the fractures needed to circulate water through superhot rock and generate electricity.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Machine learning-driven optimization of production-injection scheme: A case study of geothermal doublet system in Yangling, Guanzhong Basin
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used artificial intelligence (a computer system that learns from data) to improve how geothermal energy is extracted from hot rock formations in China. They studied a geothermal doublet system—two connected wells where hot water is pumped from one well and cooler water is returned through another—to figure out the best way to produce energy while keeping the system running efficiently over time.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Sustainable cementitious blends incorporating rice husk ash and silica flour for geothermal well applications
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have developed new types of cement blends using rice husk ash (a byproduct from rice processing) and silica flour (a fine mineral powder) that are designed to work better in geothermal wells, which are boreholes drilled deep into the Earth to access heat. These sustainable cement mixtures could improve the durability and performance of well construction in high-temperature geothermal environments.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Liquid nitrogen as a waterless fracturing fluid for enhanced geothermal systems: Mechanisms, challenges, and opportunities
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying how liquid nitrogen (extremely cold nitrogen in liquid form) could be used instead of water to crack rock deep underground for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), which are engineered reservoirs designed to extract heat from hot rock). The article examines how this waterless approach works, what problems might arise, and what potential benefits it could offer for superhot rock geothermal energy development.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Advancing geothermal reservoir temperature prediction in the Western Anatolia (Türkiye) using synthetic hydrogeochemical data from rank–Gaussian copulas
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Turkey have developed a new method to predict how hot geothermal reservoirs (underground areas containing hot water and steam) actually are by using synthetic hydrogeochemical data—information about the chemical makeup of fluids in the ground created through statistical modeling. This technique could help geothermal energy developers better understand subsurface conditions in Western Anatolia before drilling, making projects more efficient.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Preliminary Assessment of CO<sub>2</sub> Compression Behavior Modified by [BMIM][AlCl<sub>4</sub>] for Engineered Geothermal Working Fluids
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how a special chemical compound affects the behavior of carbon dioxide (CO₂) when it is compressed and used as a working fluid in engineered geothermal systems. Working fluids are substances that transfer heat from hot rocks to generate power. This research explores whether modified CO₂ could improve the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction from superhot rock reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: The potential for supercritical geothermal resources in the Taupō Volcanic Zone
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have published a study examining supercritical geothermal resources (extremely hot, high-pressure underground fluids that can generate large amounts of energy) in New Zealand's Taupō Volcanic Zone. The study explores the potential of this region to support advanced geothermal energy development by analyzing the underground conditions that could make such projects viable.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermal depletion patterns of CO<sub>2</sub> and water in closed-loop coaxial geothermal systems with vertical and L-shaped wells
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research paper examines how heat is lost over time in closed-loop geothermal systems (systems where fluid circulates continuously underground without escaping) that use either straight vertical wells or L-shaped wells. The study compares how two different heat transfer fluids—carbon dioxide and water—perform in these configurations, helping engineers understand which well designs and fluids are most efficient for extracting heat from hot rock over extended periods.

https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.title: Eavor hopes drilling tech means geothermal deeper, hotter, anywhere
https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.plain_summary: Eavor Technologies is developing a new drilling technology called Eavor-Jules that would allow geothermal systems (which extract heat from hot rocks underground) to operate much deeper and access significantly hotter temperatures. The technology could reach depths of 15 kilometers where temperatures exceed 400°C, making it possible to generate more electricity and heat from each system while reducing costs and enabling geothermal projects in regions worldwide that currently aren't suitable for this type of energy.

https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.title: Rodatherm partners with Fulcrum Point for closed-loop geothermal pilot in Utah
https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.plain_summary: Two energy companies are teaming up to build geothermal power plants in Utah using closed-loop technology, which means hot water or special fluids circulate in sealed pipes underground to generate electricity without losing water to evaporation. Their initial project aims to produce 10 megawatts of power (enough for thousands of homes), with plans to eventually expand to 200 megawatts. Rodatherm's proprietary system uses an organic working fluid instead of water and claims to be 50% more efficient than traditional geothermal methods while costing less to operate and maintain.
key_figures: $8 million grant from Emissions Reduction Alberta

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geophysic.title: Geophysical measurements completed by ENNA at Babina Greda geothermal site, Croatia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geophysic.plain_summary: A geothermal energy company completed detailed underground imaging surveys at a geothermal site in Croatia to better understand the heat potential of the area. These surveys used two types of measurements—3D seismic (sound wave mapping) and magnetotelluric (measuring natural electromagnetic fields)—to create a picture of the underground geothermal reservoir. The company plans to use this information to plan future drilling and development of the geothermal fields.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/construct.title: Construction of geothermal heating plant in Sochaczew, Poland nears completion
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/construct.plain_summary: A geothermal heating plant in Sochaczew, Poland is almost finished being built and will soon start operating. The plant uses heat pumps (devices that move heat from one place to another) and geothermal wells (deep holes that access naturally hot water underground) to provide about 40% of the city's heating from renewable sources, with backup boilers for extremely cold weather. Two wells have been drilled to depths over 1,600 meters, and the system is being funded through a major government grant.
key_figures: PLN 62 million (USD 15.63 million) total project funding

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/yeager-en.title: Yeager Energy expands geothermal business in Netherlands with third acquisition
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/yeager-en.plain_summary: Yeager Energy, a company developing geothermal projects (systems that use heat from deep underground rock), has acquired a third geothermal greenhouse company in the Netherlands called Aardwarmte Vierpolders. The company now operates four geothermal projects with a total heat output of 60 MWth (megawatts of thermal energy) and is developing five additional projects to supply heat to greenhouses, homes, and industries across Europe.
key_figures: €100 million funding from Pioneer Point Partners

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/elc-elect.title: ELC Electroconsult awarded drilling supervision contract for Ngozi geothermal project, Tanzania
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/elc-elect.plain_summary: An Italian consulting company has been hired to supervise exploratory drilling at a geothermal project in Tanzania called Ngozi. They will oversee the drilling of three slim wells (smaller-diameter wells used for initial exploration) and help train local technical staff in drilling and reservoir skills. The information gathered from these wells will help determine if Ngozi can contribute to Tanzania's goal of generating over 200 MW (megawatts, a unit of power) from geothermal sources.
key_figures: 200 MW geothermal power generation capacity target for Tanzania

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/universit.title: Universities in Aberdeen, UK partner for collaboration opportunities in geothermal
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/universit.plain_summary: Two Scottish universities have partnered to explore geothermal energy opportunities, which is technology that uses heat from deep underground rock to provide heating while reducing carbon emissions. Their collaboration will focus on research, training, and funding to develop geothermal projects in the UK, with one university recently receiving support to study whether Aberdeen could use this technology for heating.
key_figures: £1 million grant for Aberdeen Geothermal Feasibility Pilot in 2025

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/the-azore.title: The Azores will host the second edition of Geo-RIN 2027
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/the-azore.plain_summary: The Azores in Portugal will host a major geothermal energy conference in March 2027 that brings together researchers and companies from Spain and Portugal to discuss geothermal technology and innovation. The conference will cover various geothermal systems (both shallow and deep underground heat sources), next-generation technologies like Enhanced Geothermal Systems (engineered reservoirs created by fracturing hot rock), and how geothermal energy can be integrated into cities and industry. Registration is now open and researchers can submit abstracts of their work until October 2026.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pertamina.title: Pertamina Geothermal secures $75 m financing from Mizuho
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pertamina.plain_summary: An Indonesian geothermal company called Pertamina Geothermal Energy has received $75 million in financing from a Japanese bank to support its operations and future projects. The company plans to use this funding along with other recent investments to expand its geothermal capacity (the amount of electricity it can generate) significantly over the next decade.
key_figures: $477.87 million prior financing from JICA and World Bank

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/badenova-.title: Badenova, Herrenknecht finalize joint geothermal project in Hartheim, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/badenova-.plain_summary: Two German companies are partnering to build a deep geothermal heating project near Freiburg that will tap into hot rock layers approximately 3.2 kilometers underground to provide heat to around 2,000 homes. Deep geothermal energy involves drilling deep wells to access naturally hot rock formations (rather than using fossil fuels) to generate sustainable heat. The project received regulatory approval and is expected to begin drilling in late 2027.
key_figures: 2000 households to be supplied with heat

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/registrat.title: Registration open – 11th African Rift Geothermal Conference; 19-24 October 2026; Comoros
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/registrat.plain_summary: A major conference on geothermal energy in Africa is accepting registrations for October 2026 in Comoros. The event will bring together experts, policymakers, and investors to discuss how African countries can develop their geothermal resources (heat energy from within the Earth) for electricity generation and sustainable development. The program covers geology, drilling technology, power plant design, financing, and environmental concerns.
key_figures: 12 additional countries represented at previous edition

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/undergrou.title: Underground heat storage pilot in Bern, Switzerland progresses with test drilling
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/undergrou.plain_summary: A pilot project in Switzerland is testing underground heat storage using geothermal probes (pipes that exchange heat with the ground). The system will capture excess heat from a waste incineration plant during summer and store it deep underground, then retrieve it in winter to heat homes through a district heating network. Early testing has involved drilling to 400 meters depth and installing five test probes to measure how well heat conducts through the rock and soil.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/philippin.title: Philippine economy council approves $170m geothermal de-risking facility
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/philippin.plain_summary: The Philippines has approved a $170 million government fund to help reduce financial risk for companies exploring geothermal energy (heat from within the Earth used to generate electricity). The fund will cover at least half the costs of geothermal drilling and exploration, with companies only repaying the government if their exploration finds economically viable resources. This initiative aims to boost geothermal development in the Philippines, which currently ranks third globally in geothermal power capacity but has seen slower growth compared to neighboring countries.
key_figures: 50% cost coverage for exploration and drilling
3rd global ranking in installed geothermal capacity

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: A GIS-based geothermal heat cost index (GHCI) map for efficient energy planning in Europe
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers have created a digital map tool that shows where geothermal heat energy is most cost-effective across Europe. This mapping system helps cities and regions plan where to invest in geothermal projects by analyzing the expenses involved in tapping heat from underground rocks.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Uncertainty quantification under data worth for the Delft campus geothermal project
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers at Delft University studied how to measure and reduce uncertainty when deciding what data to collect for a geothermal project on their campus. They used statistical methods to figure out which measurements would be most valuable for understanding the subsurface (the rock layers below ground) and improving predictions about the geothermal system's performance.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland basin inferred from 3D conductive heat flow modelling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used computer models to map underground heat distribution in Australia's Gippsland basin to assess how much geothermal energy could be extracted there. By simulating heat flow through rock layers in three dimensions, they identified areas with the highest potential for developing geothermal resources in this region.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Quantifying geothermal heat loss at the Dayoukeng crater using UAV thermal imaging and comparison with Landsat-derived estimates
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used drone thermal imaging technology to measure heat being lost from the Dayoukeng crater, a geothermal feature, and compared their findings with satellite data from Landsat. This study helps scientists better understand and quantify the amount of thermal energy naturally radiating from geothermal sites, which is important for assessing geothermal resources.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Nigorikawa and Otake – Pioneering geothermal binary plants in Japan: Historical perspective, performance assessment, and lessons learned
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This academic article examines two pioneering geothermal power plants in Japan—Nigorikawa and Otake—that used binary cycle technology (a system where hot geothermal fluid heats a separate working fluid to spin turbines). The paper reviews their historical development, analyzes how well they performed over time, and discusses what lessons the geothermal industry can learn from their successes and challenges.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Integrated geothermometry for mixed-fluid carbonate geothermal systems under structural and hydrochemical constraints: Insights from the Yichuan Basin, central China
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how to measure underground temperatures in geothermal systems located in China's Yichuan Basin, where hot water and other fluids mix together in carbonate rock formations (porous rocks made of calcium compounds). They developed improved methods to accurately determine subsurface temperatures by considering both the rock structure and the chemical composition of fluids, which helps better understand geothermal reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Limited heat connectivity across the Northeastern Segment of the Tanlu Fault, China: Implications for low–temperature geothermal systems
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied the Tanlu Fault in northeastern China and found that heat does not flow uniformly across this geological feature, which has important consequences for developing low-temperature geothermal systems (operations that extract warmth from relatively cool underground areas) in the region. Understanding how heat moves through faults is essential for identifying the best locations to build geothermal energy projects.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Distribution characteristics and controlling factors of the thermal field and geothermal resource potential on the southern margin of the Junggar basin
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied the heat distribution and geothermal potential in the southern part of the Junggar Basin, a geological region that could be suitable for extracting energy from hot rock underground. The study identifies where the hottest rock layers are located and what natural factors control these temperature patterns, which is important information for planning future geothermal energy projects in that area.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Potential assessment of critical raw materials from European geothermal fluids
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying whether geothermal fluids—the hot water and steam that comes up from deep underground in geothermal systems—could be a source of valuable rare materials needed for electronics and other technologies. This European research explores extracting critical raw materials (like metals) from geothermal fluids, which could provide an additional economic benefit beyond just generating heat and electricity.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field-validated thermodynamic assessment of hybrid gas-removal systems for geothermal power plants
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers tested hybrid gas-removal systems (equipment that takes out unwanted gases) at real geothermal power plants to evaluate how well they work from a thermodynamic perspective (how efficiently they use heat energy). This study helps improve the performance and reliability of geothermal facilities that generate electricity from heat beneath the Earth's surface.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Tracing the source and evolution of organic matter in geothermal environments
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied how organic matter (carbon-based materials from living things and their remnants) changes and moves in geothermal environments where hot rock underground is used for energy. This research helps understand what happens to biological materials when they're exposed to the extreme heat and pressure found deep below the Earth's surface in geothermal systems.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geochemical dynamics and predictive modeling of water-rock interaction during geothermal reinjection in coal mine gobs
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how water and rock interact chemically when hot water is pumped back into abandoned coal mines for geothermal energy production. The study uses computer models to predict what happens underground when reinjection (returning used geothermal fluid) occurs in these mine spaces, helping engineers understand whether this approach could work safely and efficiently.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Optimization of well patterns for heat recovery in sedimentary geothermal systems: A hybrid GRA-COBRA approach
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers developed a new method to figure out the best way to arrange multiple wells in sedimentary geothermal systems (rock layers underground containing heat and water) to pull out heat most efficiently. The hybrid GRA-COBRA approach combines two different optimization techniques to help engineers decide where to place wells for better heat extraction performance.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Dual-porosity numerical modeling and probabilistic resource assessment of the Ulumbu geothermal field, Flores, Indonesia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers created a computer model of the Ulumbu geothermal field in Indonesia using dual-porosity modeling, which accounts for how fluids move through rock with two different types of pore spaces (tiny connected holes). The study assessed the probable amount of geothermal energy resources available at this location, helping determine whether it's viable for energy production.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Unraveling the fluid origin, circulation and heat sources of the fault-controlled Santa Teresita Geothermal System (Pipanaco basin, NW Argentina): insights from hydrochemical, isotopic and structural analysis
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied a geothermal system in Argentina to understand where its hot water comes from, how it moves through the ground, and what heats it up. They used chemical analysis of the water, isotope tracking (measuring different forms of atoms to trace water origins), and structural geology (studying rock formations and faults—cracks in the earth) to map out the system's behavior.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Field to laboratory assessment of subsurface thermal conductivity: A geothermal case study in Slovenia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Slovenia studied how well heat moves through underground rock layers by comparing measurements taken directly in the field with tests done in laboratory settings. This work helps geothermal energy projects understand the thermal properties (how heat conducts through rock) of the subsurface, which is essential for designing effective geothermal systems that extract heat from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Detecting and characterizing a hidden geothermal system in the Mt. Endut area, Indonesia, through integrated soil-gas component analyses
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Indonesia used chemical analysis of gases naturally escaping from soil to discover and map a hidden geothermal system (an underground heat source) beneath Mt. Endut. By examining the composition of these soil gases, scientists were able to characterize the location and properties of this previously unknown thermal resource.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Integrating microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP) in geothermal pavements: A coupled thermo-economic numerical evaluation
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers are studying a way to strengthen geothermal pavements (road surfaces heated by underground thermal energy) by using microorganisms to produce calcium carbonate, a natural cement-like substance. The study analyzes both the thermal performance (heat management) and economic costs of this biological strengthening method to see if it makes sense for real-world geothermal heating systems built into roads.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geothermal exploration of the Yala River segment of the Xianshuihe Fault Zone, eastern Tibetan Plateau: Insights from CSAMT surveys and deep drilling
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used advanced electromagnetic surveys (a technique that maps underground rock structures by measuring electrical properties) and deep drilling to explore geothermal potential in a fault zone on the eastern Tibetan Plateau. This work aimed to identify promising locations for geothermal energy development by understanding the subsurface geology and heat sources in the region.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: High-temperature magmatic-hydrothermal systems inferred by fumarolic fluids from Callaqui volcano, Biobio region, Chile
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied hot volcanic gases released from Callaqui volcano in Chile to understand the deep underground systems where extremely hot water and rock interact with magma (molten rock beneath Earth's surface). By analyzing the chemical composition of these gases, researchers can infer what conditions exist deep below the volcano, which helps identify potential locations for superhot rock geothermal energy development.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Petrologic and geochemical exploration of the plumbing systems under submarine volcanoes Edifice C, Three Sisters and Orca (Bransfield Strait, Antarctica)
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines the internal rock and chemical composition of underwater volcanoes in Antarctica to understand how hot fluids and magma (molten rock) move through the ground beneath them. By studying these natural volcanic systems, scientists gain insights into the subsurface structures and processes that could inform development of superhot rock geothermal energy, which harnesses extreme heat from deep underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Laboratory observations of elasto-acoustic signals of rock fragmentation, fluid-filled cavities formation, stick-slip motion and mass flux dynamics
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This scientific study examines acoustic signals (sound waves produced by rock stress) that occur when rocks break apart, when fluid-filled spaces form inside rocks, and when friction causes stick-slip motion (sudden jerky movement along surfaces). The research helps understand the physical processes happening deep underground during geothermal operations by analyzing these signals in laboratory experiments.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Hydrothermal alteration facies model and its link to rock mechanics - A comparative analysis of andesitic volcanoes in New Zealand
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines how volcanic rocks in New Zealand change their physical properties when exposed to hot, mineral-rich fluids underground—a process called hydrothermal alteration. The study compares how these chemical changes affect the mechanical strength and behavior of andesite rock (a common volcanic rock type), which is important for understanding how rocks behave at depth in geothermal systems.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Alteration pathways of the Serra Geral Group basalts and their controls on the petrophysical properties of volcanic reservoirs
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This research examines how volcanic rock from the Serra Geral Group breaks down and changes over time, and how these changes affect the rock's ability to store and transmit fluids—properties crucial for using volcanic reservoirs as geothermal resources. The study identifies the specific pathways through which these basalt rocks (a type of volcanic rock) transform and explains what controls these transformations, providing insights relevant to developing geothermal energy in volcanic regions.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: The Rotokawa geothermal system, New Zealand: Hydrothermal minerals and punctuated evolution
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This academic paper examines the Rotokawa geothermal system in New Zealand, focusing on the minerals formed by hot water moving through rock and how the system has changed over time through distinct evolutionary phases. Understanding these mineral deposits and system changes helps researchers better characterize geothermal reservoirs.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Isotopic evidence for slab-derived magmatic water beneath the Kussharo Caldera, Japan
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studying the Kussharo Caldera in Japan found chemical evidence that water trapped in the deep rock layers comes from subducting oceanic plates (slabs of Earth's crust sinking into the mantle). This discovery helps scientists understand how water moves through volcanic regions and could inform geothermal energy exploration by revealing where hot water resources exist underground.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geo-THM characterization for safe CO<sub>2</sub> storage and geothermal energy in karstified-fractured carbonates: A reservoir and geomechanical risk management framework
Modelling hot water and power production from a low-enthalpy geothermal carbonate reservoir; South Swan Hills, Alberta, Canada
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how to extract heat and generate electricity from a warm rock reservoir in Alberta, Canada that contains carbonate rock (a type of rock made from calcium-based minerals). The project models whether this lower-temperature geothermal resource could be practical for power production, focusing on understanding the underground conditions that affect how much hot water can be pumped out and used.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Transient thermal performance of U-loop geothermal systems with dual-borehole lateral sections using a computationally efficient framework
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers developed a fast computer model to predict how U-shaped pipes (a common underground heat exchange design where pipes loop down and back up) perform when they have two boreholes—holes drilled into the ground—with horizontal sections extending sideways. This model helps engineers understand how temperature changes over time in these geothermal systems, which is important for designing efficient heating and cooling systems that use Earth's heat.

https://www.edengeothermal.com/2026/07/2.title: Eden Geothermal Speaks at Kings College London
https://www.edengeothermal.com/2026/07/2.plain_summary: Eden Geothermal participated in a speaking event at King's College London focused on how to gain public support for deep geothermal energy projects (energy extracted from hot rock deep underground). The company shared lessons learned from their own geothermal project and discussed findings about public perceptions of this technology, alongside other experts in the field.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/eoi-agenc.title: EOI – Agencies for geothermal assessment, development in Andaman & Nicobar Islands, India
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/eoi-agenc.plain_summary: India's government energy company is seeking qualified organizations to help assess and develop geothermal energy projects in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, a remote territory that currently depends heavily on imported fossil fuels. The region has been identified as having suitable underground geological conditions for tapping into Earth's heat as a renewable energy source. The government wants partners with expertise in exploring geothermal resources, drilling wells, mapping underground rock layers, and building power generation systems.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/nlr-highl.title: NLR highlights licensable technologies for deeper, more profitable geothermal drilling
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/nlr-highl.plain_summary: The National Laboratory of the Rockies has identified three ready-to-use technologies that could make geothermal drilling deeper and more cost-effective. These include a high-temperature power generator that works in extreme heat, specialized sensors and electronics that collect drilling data in harsh conditions, and software that predicts costs for new geothermal projects. These innovations are already available for geothermal companies to license and use.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.title: Geothermal exploration permit in Guadeloupe granted to Albioma
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.plain_summary: A French energy company called Albioma has received permission to explore for geothermal resources (heat from deep underground rock) at a site in Guadeloupe. Over the next five years, they will study existing geological data, conduct surface surveys, and create models to determine if there is a high-temperature geothermal reservoir (an underground area containing hot rock suitable for energy production) in the region. The company will need to apply separately for drilling permission if their exploration is successful.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: From magnetic anomaly to geothermal resource: An updated Curie depth map for the geothermal assessment of Colombia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers in Colombia have created an updated map showing the depth of the Curie point—the depth in the Earth where rocks lose their magnetic properties due to extreme heat—to help identify promising locations for geothermal energy development. By analyzing magnetic data from the region, scientists can now better pinpoint areas where rocks underground are hot enough to be useful for geothermal energy production.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/strataphy.title: Strataphy, TAQA Geothermal partner to accelerate geothermal cooling deployment in Saudi Arabia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/strataphy.plain_summary: Two companies have partnered to bring geothermal cooling technology to Saudi Arabia. TAQA Geothermal will handle project management and development, while Strataphy contributes its PrimeLoop® technology—a ground-based cooling system that uses heat from beneath the earth's surface to cool buildings without needing water. The partnership aims to expand this sustainable cooling approach across the country to reduce electricity consumption.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/burghause.title: Burghausen, Germany to invest €27m to build geothermal heating network
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/burghause.plain_summary: The city of Burghausen in Germany is investing €27 million to build a heating network that will deliver geothermal heat (heat extracted from hot rock beneath the Earth's surface) from a nearby geothermal plant to homes and buildings in the city. A 10-kilometer pipeline is being constructed to transport this heat, with the system expected to start operating by 2028, helping the city reduce carbon emissions and transition to more sustainable heating.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/small-sca.title: Small-scale hydropower and geothermal power project implemented in Taitung, Taiwan
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/small-sca.plain_summary: A pilot project in Taiwan combined small-scale hydropower (electricity generated from flowing water) with a geothermal thermoelectric generator (a device that converts heat from hot springs into electricity) to produce power at a hot spring resort. Though the total output is modest, the project demonstrates how communities can generate their own renewable energy and provides educational value, with potential to be replicated at other hot spring locations across Taiwan.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/gros-scho.title: Groß Schönebeck geothermal research site in Germany celebrates 25th anniversary
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/gros-scho.plain_summary: A research facility in Germany called Groß Schönebeck has been studying geothermal energy (heat from deep underground rocks) for 25 years, using a converted old natural gas well. Scientists there have developed important techniques for finding and accessing geothermal resources, including methods to map underground rock structures and measure their properties. Recently, they're testing new technology that can extract heat directly from deep boreholes without pumping water to the surface, which could make geothermal energy more practical and scalable worldwide.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pakistan-.title: Pakistan moves toward developing lithium extraction technology for geothermal brine
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/pakistan-.plain_summary: Pakistan's state energy company has discovered lithium (a mineral used in batteries) in hot, salty water from a geothermal well in the Sindh region. They've partnered with a nuclear research institute to develop technology for extracting lithium from this geothermal brine (salt water heated deep underground). If successful, this could provide Pakistan with access to a valuable resource while also demonstrating how geothermal systems can be used for more than just energy production.
key_figures: 8 to 10 additional wells identified for exploration

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.title: Geothermal exploration drilling starts in Nowy Dwór Mazowiecki, Poland
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.plain_summary: A new geothermal exploration well has begun drilling in Poland to test whether hot water beneath the city can be used for heating and other purposes. The well will go down about 2,070 meters to reach the thermal water deposits. The project received government funding and is expected to cost approximately 12.9 million Polish zloty.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/85-degree.title: 85 Degrees secures €200m financing for geothermal heating projects in the Netherlands
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/85-degree.plain_summary: A renewable heat company called 85 Degrees has secured €200 million in financing from two major banks to develop geothermal heating projects in the Netherlands. These projects will extract heat from hot rock layers underground to supply greenhouses, reducing their need for natural gas. The company has already drilled five wells in one area and plans to expand this heating infrastructure across the country.
key_figures: 5 wells drilled in Bleiswijk study area

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/mou-signe.title: MoU signed for first open-space cooling geothermal system in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/mou-signe.plain_summary: A major agreement has been signed to build the world's first geothermal cooling system for open spaces at a university campus in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The PrimeLoop technology pumps heat into the earth rather than cooling towers that spray water into the air, which means it uses zero water and cuts electricity needs by up to half—a huge benefit in a water-scarce region. This project demonstrates how shallow geothermal (heat from underground rock layers) can cool large areas sustainably and efficiently.
key_figures: 50% electricity reduction compared to conventional cooling

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/gdc-break.title: GDC breaks ground on geothermal laboratory in Nakuru County, Kenya
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/gdc-break.plain_summary: Kenya's Geothermal Development Company has started building a new science laboratory at its facility in Nakuru County to improve how it studies and manages geothermal resources (heat and energy from underground rock). The lab will conduct geological analysis (studying rock types and composition) and help the company better understand underground reservoirs (pockets of hot water and steam), replacing temporary facilities they've used for 17 years.
key_figures: 105 MW installed capacity target at Menengai steam field

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.title: Drilling contract signed for second doublet for AFK geothermal heating project, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.plain_summary: A German geothermal heating company has hired a drilling contractor to build a second deep geothermal system (called a doublet—two connected wells that extract and return hot water) to expand heat service to nearby communities. The new wells will tap into hot water at about 89°C from 2,700 meters underground, which will be circulated through heat exchangers to warm homes and businesses, then returned to the ground through a second well.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/266m-to-b.title: $266m to be invested to restore full capacity of Sarulla geothermal power plant, Indonesia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/266m-to-b.plain_summary: Indonesia is investing approximately $267 million to restore a major geothermal power plant in North Sumatra called Sarulla back to its full operating capacity of 330 megawatts (a unit of electrical power). The plant is currently producing only 220 megawatts because underground steam pressure in the geothermal reservoir—the hot rock layer beneath the surface that provides the heat—has changed. Work on this restoration is scheduled to begin in 2027 after administrative approvals are completed.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/energy-in.title: Energy investment firm considers investing in Furusato Netsuden geothermal projects in Japan
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/energy-in.plain_summary: An investment firm called HEXA Energy Services has agreed to explore funding opportunities with Furusato Netsuden, a Japanese company that develops geothermal power plants (facilities that generate electricity from heat deep underground). The two companies plan to work together to expand geothermal energy projects in Japan, combining HEXA's investment expertise with Furusato Netsuden's experience building and operating these plants.
key_figures: 16 years since previous 1+ MW plant commissioned in Japan (as of 2015)

https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/geo.title: How to bring a geothermal well back from the dead
https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/geo.plain_summary: A geothermal company called Zanskar purchased an underperforming power plant in New Mexico that was losing heat from its shallow wells (boreholes that tap into Earth's warmth underground). The company is working to restore the plant's productivity, essentially reviving geothermal infrastructure that had begun to fail.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Effects of reservoir permeability heterogeneity on the size of solute and thermal protection zone around a geothermal reinjection well in a porous reservoir, Hungary
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This scientific research examines how uneven distribution of permeability (the ability of rock to let fluids flow through it) in underground reservoirs affects the safety zones around wells where cooled geothermal water is pumped back into the ground. The study, conducted in Hungary, looks at how these protection zones change depending on the rock's varying flow characteristics.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geothermal cell connectivity between Cerro Pabellón Dome and Apacheta-Aguilucho Volcanic complex (northern Chile) as confirmed by noble gas monitoring
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used noble gases (rare gases naturally present in the Earth) to track connections between two geothermal systems in northern Chile: Cerro Pabellón Dome and Apacheta-Aguilucho Volcanic complex. This monitoring technique helps scientists understand how hot fluids and gases move underground between different geothermal reservoirs (underground formations containing hot water and steam), which is important for developing geothermal energy resources in the region.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Stratigraphic and thermal constraints on the evolution of zeolite zonation in continental flood basalts: Insights from the Serra Geral Group, Paraná–Etendeka Magmatic Province
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied how minerals called zeolites formed and changed positions in ancient volcanic rock layers in Brazil, examining how temperature and rock structure influenced this process. Understanding zeolite distribution in these flood basalts (massive layers of hardened lava) can provide insights into subsurface conditions and rock properties relevant to geothermal exploration.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Multi-energy liquid air energy storage powered by geothermal energy from an abandoned exploitation well – A techno-economic analysis
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied a system that combines liquid air energy storage (a method of storing energy by cooling air to extremely cold temperatures) with geothermal heat from old, unused oil and gas wells. The analysis examines whether this combination is technically practical and economically worthwhile, exploring how abandoned wells could be repurposed to support renewable energy systems.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Energy and Exergy Analysis of Geothermal–ORC Hybrid Trigeneration System with a Self-Superheater using Low-GWP Working Fluids
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers analyzed a hybrid system that combines geothermal energy with an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC), which is a heat engine that converts thermal energy into electricity using special working fluids. The system includes a self-superheater (a device that further heats the working fluid) and uses low-GWP fluids (refrigerants designed to minimize environmental impact). The study examined both energy efficiency and exergy (the maximum useful work that can be extracted from energy) to evaluate how well this combined system could generate power, heating, and cooling simultaneously.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/blm-appro.title: BLM approves drilling in Utah as part of study on blind geothermal systems
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/blm-appro.plain_summary: The U.S. government has approved drilling in Utah as part of a research project called INGENIOUS that aims to find hidden geothermal systems—geothermal resources with no obvious surface signs like hot springs. Scientists will drill shallow boreholes (underground holes) to about 800 feet deep to measure temperature patterns and identify potential geothermal energy sources that aren't visible from the surface, helping reduce exploration costs and risks for future geothermal development.
key_figures: 8-10 locations to be selected for drilling

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/green-the.title: Green Therma signs drilling contract for closed-loop geothermal demonstration in Denmark
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/green-the.plain_summary: Green Therma has hired a drilling company to build a deep geothermal well in Denmark as part of a demonstration project for their Heat4Ever technology, which is a closed-loop system (meaning water circulates in a sealed loop underground and transfers heat without escaping) that extracts heat from hot rock to supply district heating. The well will reach about 4 kilometers straight down and then 3 kilometers horizontally, making it Denmark's deepest geothermal well, with drilling expected to start in January 2027 and funded by approximately $11 million from Denmark's government.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.title: Drilling of 3.9-km geothermal well in Banska Nizna, Poland completed
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/drilling-.plain_summary: A geothermal well called Banska PGP-7 has been successfully drilled to a depth of nearly 3.9 kilometers in Poland. Once testing is complete, the well is expected to supply geothermal heat (warmth extracted from hot rocks underground) to homes and buildings in the local region through a district heating system by late 2026.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/utah-forg.title: Utah FORGE starts extended circulation test to evaluate long-term Enhanced Geothermal performance
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/utah-forg.plain_summary: Utah FORGE, a research project studying superhot rock geothermal technology, has started a long-term test of an Enhanced Geothermal System (EGS)—a method that artificially creates heat reservoirs by fracturing rock and circulating water through it. The test will pump water between two wells for roughly 90 days (possibly extended to 120 days) to study how well these systems perform over time, particularly focusing on temperature loss and water leakage, which are key challenges for making this technology commercially profitable.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/californi.title: California appeals court questions environmental review of geothermal lithium project
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/californi.plain_summary: A California appeals court ruled that a geothermal and lithium extraction project in Imperial County did not receive adequate environmental review, particularly regarding potential air quality impacts and water availability concerns. The court did confirm that the company properly consulted with local Native American tribes about the project's effects on cultural sites.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/cornish-l.title: Cornish Lithium receives grant funding to advance Cross Lanes geothermal lithium project
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/cornish-l.plain_summary: A UK company called Cornish Lithium received £7.2 million in government funding to drill wells and test technology for extracting lithium from hot underground water in Cornwall. The company previously found water at 2000 meters depth that was hot enough (70°C) and contained lithium (a valuable mineral used in batteries). With this funding, they plan to drill two more wells and test a Direct Lithium Extraction system, which is a process to pull lithium out of geothermal water, while also exploring nearby areas for additional lithium deposits.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/ongc-comp.title: ONGC completes drilling of second geothermal well at Puga Valley in India
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/ongc-comp.plain_summary: India's state oil company ONGC has successfully drilled a second exploratory well at Puga Valley in the mountainous Ladakh region to support a planned geothermal power project. The well, drilled to 1,000 meters depth, was completed in about a month and follows an earlier well that took much longer due to challenges like the high-altitude location. The two wells will support a small pilot power plant that aims to generate electricity from heat naturally present deep underground.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/early-wor.title: Early work completed for geothermal heating project in Novi Sad, Serbia
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/early-wor.plain_summary: The Serbian city of Novi Sad is building a geothermal heating plant in the Miseluk neighborhood, which uses heat from beneath the earth's surface to warm buildings. Geological surveys have been completed and the first exploration well has been drilled, with a second well currently under construction.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/uplift-pr.title: UPLIFT project seeks to develop and demonstrate safe Enhanced Geothermal for Europe
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/uplift-pr.plain_summary: The UPLIFT project is a four-year European research initiative launching in 2026 to safely test enhanced geothermal systems (EGS)—a method of extracting heat from hot rocks deep underground by artificially creating fractures to improve water flow. The project will develop new drilling techniques and computer simulations to make this technology work better in European geological conditions while reducing earthquake risks and gaining public support, with practical demonstrations at a test site in Czechia.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Synergistic effects of epoxy/PTFE/CNT hybrid nanocomposite coating against silica scaling and corrosion under varying geothermal flow conditions
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers developed a special protective coating made from epoxy (a type of plastic), PTFE (a slippery material), and carbon nanotubes (extremely tiny carbon structures) to protect equipment used in geothermal systems. The coating was tested to see how well it could prevent two common problems: silica scaling (mineral buildup) and corrosion (metal degradation) when geothermal fluid flows through equipment under different conditions.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Entraining low-pressure geothermal fluid for power generation using a supersonic ejector: A case study from Theistareykir power plant
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied a method to generate electricity from geothermal fluid that has relatively low pressure (meaning it's at a less intense energy state) at Iceland's Theistareykir power plant. They used a supersonic ejector—a device that accelerates fluid to very high speeds to mix and combine different geothermal streams more efficiently. This technique could help extract more useful energy from geothermal resources that might otherwise be harder to exploit for power generation.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Corrigendum to “3-D Magnetotelluric Modeling and Radiogenic Heat Reservoir for EGS Development: A Case Study of the Kestanbol Granitoid Intrusion (NW Türkiye)” [Geothermics, 140 (2026) 103728]
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: This is a correction notice for a previously published scientific paper about using magnetotelluric imaging (a technique that maps underground rock properties using electromagnetic measurements) to study a granite rock formation in northwestern Turkey for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) development, which is a method to create geothermal reservoirs in hot rock where natural water doesn't exist.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/research-.title: Research projects seeks to study geothermal suitability of limestone in Rhine-Ruhr region, Germany
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/research-.plain_summary: Researchers in Germany are studying whether limestone rock formations in the Rhine-Ruhr region are suitable for extracting geothermal heat (thermal energy from deep underground). Limestone in this area has natural cracks and channels that allow hot fluids to flow, but chemical reactions can damage the rock and infrastructure over time. The three-year research project will map suitable locations, test how rock and fluids interact, and create computer tools to help energy companies plan and evaluate geothermal projects in the region.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/ipeks-geo.title: Ipeks Geothermal to drill 13 wells for geothermal greenhouse in Afyonkarahisar, Türkiye
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/ipeks-geo.plain_summary: A Turkish geothermal company plans to drill 13 new wells in Afyonkarahisar to expand its geothermal greenhouse operations, which currently use hot water from existing wells to heat crops. The new wells will include 10 production wells (to extract hot geothermal fluid from underground) and 3 reinjection wells (to return cooled fluid back into the ground), and will reach depths of about 1,330 meters to access hotter rocks below the surface.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/new-york-.title: New York City embarks on study to build thermal energy network around subway stations
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/new-york-.plain_summary: New York City is studying whether to build a thermal energy network around subway stations that would use geothermal boreholes (deep holes drilled into the ground) to capture excess heat from hot subway platforms during summer and store it underground for use heating nearby city buildings in winter. The project would use radiant cooling technology to pull heat from platforms and transfer it through boreholes beneath Chambers Street, reducing platform temperatures and lowering energy costs.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/bmwe-prog.title: BMWE programme to highlight young, innovative geothermal companies at GeoTHERM 2027
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/bmwe-prog.plain_summary: Germany's government is offering funding to help young geothermal companies afford booth space at an upcoming industry conference called GeoTHERM 2027, happening in February. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/hybrid-ge.title: Hybrid geothermal + biogas industrial heating system starts operations in Shandong, China
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/hybrid-ge.plain_summary: A facility in China has begun using a combination of geothermal energy (heat from deep underground) and biogas to produce steam for industrial heating. The geothermal water from medium depths pre-heats water before biogas burns to create the final steam, reducing reliance on expensive gas-fired boilers while cutting coal consumption and carbon emissions significantly.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/contract-.title: Contract signed for construction of local geothermal heating network in Szaflary, Poland
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/contract-.plain_summary: A Polish community is building a local heating network that will distribute geothermal heat (warmth extracted from hot underground rocks and water) from a deep well called Banska PGP-4 to homes and buildings starting in 2026. The well has already been drilled very deep and tested, showing it contains hot water at high temperatures suitable for heating. Before heat delivery can begin, some repairs are needed inside the well where its diameter has become narrower, and official approvals must be obtained.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/project-i.title: Project InnerSpace and SPE partner to strengthen technical focus on geothermal
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/project-i.plain_summary: Project InnerSpace and the Society of Petroleum Engineers (SPE), a professional organization for engineers in the oil and gas industry, are partnering to make geothermal energy a formal technical focus area. The partnership includes a $100,000 grant to fund initiatives that help oil and gas professionals apply their existing drilling, engineering, and technical skills to develop geothermal energy, which harnesses heat from deep underground rocks to generate power.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: 2D magnetotelluric inversion and 3D resistivity visualization for geothermal system characterization: A case study of Mount Parakasak
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used magnetotelluric inversion (a technique that measures how rock layers respond to natural electromagnetic signals) and 3D resistivity visualization (creating detailed maps of how well different rock types conduct electricity) to study the geothermal system beneath Mount Parakasak. This approach helps scientists understand the underground structure and heat potential of geothermal sites.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Imaging the resistivity structure of Nage Geothermal System, Flores Island, Indonesia through 3-D magnetotelluric inversion incorporating the sea effect
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used a technique called magnetotelluric inversion (which maps electrical resistance patterns underground) to study the Nage Geothermal System in Indonesia. They created a 3-D model of the subsurface to understand the geothermal resource, accounting for the effect of nearby seawater on their electrical measurements.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Enhancing identification of geothermal prospection in Yingshan geothermal field using machine learning and thermal infrared remote sensing
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used computer learning algorithms and thermal imaging from satellites to better identify promising locations for geothermal energy development in China's Yingshan geothermal field. By analyzing heat patterns visible from above and using artificial intelligence to process the data, they improved the ability to spot underground areas with potential for geothermal resource extraction.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Thermal diffusivity and transient thermal response of the Sabatini volcanic succession: insights from the shallow geothermal field at the ENEA-Casaccia Research Centre (Roma, Italy)
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how heat moves through volcanic rocks at a shallow geothermal research site in Rome, Italy. By measuring thermal diffusivity (the speed at which heat spreads through rock), they gained insights into how these volcanic materials respond to temperature changes, which is useful for understanding geothermal systems in volcanic regions.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: A first seismic constraint of Pantelleria's shallowest crust (southern Italy): The 1D shear-wave velocity model
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Scientists studied the structure of shallow rock layers beneath Pantelleria, an island in southern Italy, using seismic waves (vibrations that travel through the earth) to create a map of how fast those waves move through different rock types. This type of underground mapping helps researchers understand the geological conditions in volcanic areas that might be relevant for geothermal energy exploration.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Geoelectrical characterization of fumarolic activity zones at Cerro Machín Volcano, central Colombia
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers used electrical measurement techniques to study hot steam vents (fumaroles) at a volcano in Colombia, mapping underground zones where geothermal heat is concentrated. This type of electrical mapping helps identify where hot rock resources might be located beneath volcanoes, which is relevant for understanding geothermal potential in volcanic regions.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.title: Heat transfer characteristics of an oceanic crust thermal reservoir under seawater cyclic thermal shock: optimization for geothermal energy extraction
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/ar.plain_summary: Researchers studied how heat moves through oceanic crust (the rocky layer beneath the ocean floor) when it experiences repeated temperature changes from seawater, which is relevant for extracting geothermal energy from the ocean floor. The study focuses on optimizing how to best extract heat from this type of thermal reservoir (a naturally hot rock formation) for energy production.

https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.title: Old Dutch Foods Opens New Energy-Efficient Facility in Prince Edward Island
https://www.geothermalcanada.org/news/20.plain_summary: A snack food company opened a new office and warehouse building in Prince Edward Island that uses geothermal technology (a system that exchanges heat with the ground through boreholes to heat and cool the building) as its main heating and cooling source, along with solar panels and an air recovery system. The facility uses no fossil fuels and produces zero carbon emissions, demonstrating the company's commitment to environmentally responsible operations.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.title: Geothermal could transform the UK energy industry
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.plain_summary: The UK could reduce its reliance on imported natural gas by developing geothermal energy—heat extracted from deep underground—which would improve energy security and lower carbon emissions. The country has valuable expertise from decades of oil and gas drilling in the North Sea that could be redirected to access geothermal resources. A recent estimate suggests the UK's geothermal potential could meet heating demands for a century, and the National Geothermal Centre is working with government, companies, and universities to create a roadmap for making geothermal a standard part of Britain's low-carbon energy system.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/portland-.title: Portland State leads initiative on siting Enhanced Geothermal projects using AI
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/portland-.plain_summary: Portland State University is leading a research project that uses artificial intelligence to help identify the best locations for Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS)—a technology that taps into extremely hot rock deep underground to generate electricity. Over the next four years, the project will map underground resources, create guidelines to remove barriers to development, and build a digital platform to monitor geothermal installations.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/edc-plans.title: EDC plans capacity increase via modernization of Palinpinon geothermal power plant in Philippines
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/edc-plans.plain_summary: A major Philippine energy company is upgrading an existing geothermal power plant (a facility that taps heat from deep underground rocks to generate electricity) to produce more power without needing to extract additional steam from the ground. The upgrade will replace older turbine generators with more powerful newer models, increasing the plant's output from 112.5 MW to 126 MW and extending its operational life by several years. The company is also planning a larger redevelopment project at another site that could create a new plant with 200 to 400 MW of capacity, demonstrating that geothermal resources can support decades of continuous energy production.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/maren-mar.title: Maren Maras plans 99-MW geothermal power development in Aydin, Türkiye
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/maren-mar.plain_summary: A Turkish energy company is planning to build three geothermal power plants in Aydin that will generate electricity from heat in the Earth's crust. The plants will use binary cycle technology (a method that converts geothermal heat into electricity) and are expected to produce enough power for hundreds of thousands of homes annually. The project involves drilling multiple wells to access hot rock underground and pump geothermal fluid to the surface.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/tender-in.title: Tender – Infrastructure and equipment for geothermal slim hole drilling in Grenada
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/tender-in.plain_summary: Grenada's government is seeking bids for construction work needed before drilling two exploratory geothermal wells (boreholes used to test for heat beneath the earth). The work includes building roads, water systems, and electrical equipment at two drilling sites. If successful, this project could eventually lead to a 15-megawatt power plant (a facility generating electricity) that would supply nearly half of Grenada's electricity needs.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/draft-gui.title: Draft guidelines for Philippine geothermal de-risking facility opened for public consultation
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/draft-gui.plain_summary: The Philippines has created a new funding program called the Philippine Geothermal Resource Derisking Facility to help companies explore for geothermal energy (heat from deep underground rock). The program provides loans to cover half the costs of early exploration work like drilling test wells, with companies contributing the other half. If drilling shows the site isn't commercially viable, the loan converts to a grant, meaning no repayment is required.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/a-new-era.title: A New Era in Geothermal Investment: IGIS 2026 to be held 26-27 November in Cappadocia, Türkiye
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/a-new-era.plain_summary: An international conference called IGIS 2026 will bring together investors, companies, and geothermal experts in Turkey in November 2026 to discuss the future of geothermal energy. The summit will focus on emerging technologies including closed-loop geothermal systems (where fluid circulates continuously through hot rock without being extracted), ways to access deep hot rock resources, and new business models for using geothermal energy in agriculture, industry, and tourism alongside electricity generation.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/full-stea.title: Full Steam Ahead: women in geothermal, premiering at RIFF
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/full-stea.plain_summary: A documentary film called 'Full Steam Ahead' is premiering at the Reykjavík International Film Festival, following women working in geothermal energy (heat from the Earth used for power) across Iceland, Japan, and Kenya. The film explores the barriers women face in this male-dominated industry and highlights how visibility through mentors and role models can help more women enter and advance in geothermal careers. The filmmakers found that despite progress in hiring more women in technical roles, they still struggle to reach senior leadership positions globally.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.title: Geothermal Rising announces winners of inaugural Tech Awards
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/geotherma.plain_summary: Geothermal Rising, an industry organization, has announced the first winners of its Tech Awards program, which recognizes new technologies that solve major challenges in geothermal energy development. The winning technologies address key areas like drilling (the process of creating wells into the earth), fracturing rocks to release heat, turbine efficiency, and mapping underground conditions. These awards aim to highlight innovations that make geothermal projects cheaper, less risky, and easier to build in more locations.

https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/regulator.title: Regulatory stability and financing structures for geothermal highlighted at Budapest summit
https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/regulator.plain_summary: Leaders from Europe and beyond gathered at a conference in Budapest to discuss how geothermal energy—heat extracted from within the Earth—can help meet climate goals and provide reliable energy. Speakers emphasized that governments need to create stable, predictable policies to attract investment, and that different financing strategies are needed for different stages of geothermal projects. They noted that geothermal technology is ready to deploy across a wide range of depths and applications, but success depends on long-term government commitment and access to capital.
